blocks.text: A complex ion has a central metal ion bonded to surrounding electron-donating species. The metal ion acts as a Lewis acid (electron-pair acceptor) and molecules or ions with lone pairs, such as H2O, NH3, Cl- and OH-, act as Lewis bases. The number of coordinate bonds to the metal ion is the coordination number; common values are 2, 4 and 6.

Complex formation is more typical of transition metals, which have available d orbitals, but Group 2 ions can also form complexes, especially those at the top of the group. Smaller ions have a higher charge density and attract donor species better, and all Group 2 ions carry a +2 charge.

items: Hydrated ions: when Group 2 salts dissolve, the ions are hydrated, water acting as the electron-pair donor. Be2+, the smallest, forms [Be(H2O)4]2+ (coordination number 4); Mg2+ forms [Mg(H2O)6]2+ (coordination number 6); Ca2+, Sr2+ and Ba2+ also mostly have coordination number 6, with weaker interaction down the group.

blocks.alt: Structure of the hydrated magnesium ion: Mg in the centre with six OH2 groups, one above, one below and four around it (two drawn with hashed bonds going back, two with wedges coming forward), inside square brackets with charge 2+, and a sulphate ion, SO4 2-, beside it.
blocks.caption: Structure of [Mg(H2O)6]2+ with a sulphate ion (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered structure).

items: Chelates: ions, especially the smaller ones, form stable complexes with donors that have more than one donor pair, which make several bonds to the same ion and form rings. Ca2+ forms a ring complex with EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid), a six-pair donor: Ca2+ + EDTA4- -> [Ca(EDTA)]2-. EDTA is used to soften water by removing Ca2+ and Mg2+, and in medicine to remove toxic metal ions from the body.
